content: The following is a professional summary of the findings from various studies assessing the impact of animal-source foods (ASF) on dietary and health outcomes in children: 1. Egg Consumption and Growth Outcomes: Studies by Iannotti et al. (2017) and Stewart et al. (2019) evaluated the impact of daily egg consumption (1 egg/day for 6 months) on growth outcomes in children aged 6–9 months. Children consuming eggs showed significant improvements in height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) and head circumference-for-age z-scores (HCAZ) compared to those who did not consume eggs. However, no significant differences were observed in weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), or stunting rates. The quality of evidence was rated as low to very low. 2. Egg Consumption and Micronutrient Outcomes: Makrides et al. (2002) assessed the impact of consuming 4 egg yolks per week on anemia, hemoglobin concentration, serum ferritin levels, and transferrin receptor levels in breastfed and formula-fed children over 6 months. No significant differences were observed in these outcomes between children consuming egg yolks and those who did not. The quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate. 3. Egg Consumption and Fatty Acid Levels: Hoffman et al. (2004) reported a significant increase in docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) levels in children consuming dried egg yolks compared to those who did not. However, no significant differences were observed in eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) or linoleic acid (LA) levels. 4. Fish Consumption and Fatty Acid Levels: Libuda et al. (2016) found that children consuming fish had significantly higher EPA levels and lower LA levels compared to those who did not consume fish. No significant differences were observed in alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) levels. 5. Caterpillar Consumption and Growth Outcomes: Bauserman et al. (2015) evaluated the impact of caterpillar cereal consumption (30–45 g/day) on growth outcomes in children aged 6–18 months. No significant differences were observed in stunting, wasting, WAZ, HAZ, or WHZ between children consuming caterpillar cereal and those who did not. However, children consuming caterpillar cereal showed a significant reduction in anemia and an increase in hemoglobin concentration. Serum ferritin levels were significantly lower in the caterpillar group, while transferrin receptor levels were similar between groups. 6. Cow’s Milk Consumption and Micronutrient Outcomes: Thorsdottir et al. (2003) assessed the impact of consuming >500 g/day of cow’s milk on hemoglobin concentration, serum ferritin levels, and transferrin receptor levels in children aged 9–12 months. No significant differences were observed in these outcomes between children consuming higher versus lower amounts of cow’s milk. 7. Variety of ASF and Stunting: Krasovec et al. (2017) and Marinda et al. (2018) reported that children consuming a greater variety of ASF (e.g., 2–3 types) had significantly lower rates of stunting compared to those consuming fewer or no types of ASF. The quality of evidence was rated as low. 8. Summary of Findings: Across 31 studies, the most commonly reported outcomes were stunting, wasting, underweight, WAZ, HAZ, WHZ, anemia, hemoglobin concentration, vitamin B12 levels, and ferritin levels. The evidence suggests that ASF consumption may have some benefits for growth and micronutrient outcomes, but the quality of evidence was generally low to moderate. Most findings were based on single studies, and high heterogeneity among studies limited the ability to perform meta-analyses. 9. Limitations: The studies included in this review were of varying quality, with many relying on observational designs. There was also limited evidence on the effects of processed versus fresh ASF, and high heterogeneity among studies made it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. In conclusion, while some benefits of ASF consumption on growth and micronutrient outcomes were observed, the overall quality of evidence was low, and further high-quality research is needed to confirm these findings.
